slides.title: Chapter 24: Make Python Talk
slides.say: This chapter is about a program that speaks, writes down what it hears, and makes subtitles. It has sixteen examples, and all of them run on the chapter page in the order of this deck. Nothing is heard: the machine of the examples has no sound card, so pyttsx3 writes WAV files and no sound is played. A public-domain reading of the Gettysburg Address from the Internet Archive stands in for a video site, and nothing is downloaded from YouTube. Windows and macOS were not run. The route on slide 2 shows the five parts.

slides.title: Today's route through five parts
slides.say: The chapter has five parts. Part 1 prints the versions and queues and speaks a sentence. Part 2 changes the voice, the rate and the volume and saves speech as a WAV file. Part 3 turns audio into text with Whisper models and shows what the models need. Part 4 writes subtitle files and reads and downloads audio with yt-dlp. Part 5 builds the three practice programs. Each part has concept slides, a story with a picture, and code slides with a measured result. The summary on slide 41 and the links on slide 42 close the chapter.

slides.title: Two questions this chapter answers
slides.say: Two questions frame the chapter. The first asks how a program speaks and where the sound goes when the machine has no sound card. Parts 1 and 2 answer it with a queue that runAndWait() speaks and with WAV files that save_to_file() writes, and the summary on slide 41 repeats it. The second asks how a program turns audio into text and subtitles and which calls wait for ever or fail quietly. Parts 3 and 4 answer the first half, the table on slide 39 collects the quiet surprises, and the practice questions on slide 40 check both.

slides.title: Part 1: The tools and the speech engine
slides.say: Part 1 starts with the tools, because every example needs three packages and two programs outside Python. The first example prints their versions and asks whether ffmpeg, eSpeak NG and a sound device are there. The second example makes an engine, queues a sentence and shows that the queue is spoken only when runAndWait() runs. It also shows that a second runAndWait() in the same process does not come back. The concept slides 5 and 6 explain the names, and slide 7 tells the story of the first speaking machine.

slides.title: The tools: modules and programs
slides.say: Three packages and two programs do the work of this chapter. pyttsx3 makes speech, whisper turns audio into text, and yt_dlp reads and downloads from web pages. json and pathlib are standard modules that the programs use for data and files. eSpeak NG is the speech system that pyttsx3 uses on Linux, SAPI5 is the one of Windows and NSSpeechSynthesizer is the one of macOS. FFmpeg converts audio and video, and both Whisper and yt-dlp call it. Compare slide 8, which prints the versions that ran.

slides.title: Text to speech: the engine and its calls
slides.say: The engine has three calls in a row. pyttsx3.init() returns the engine of the platform's speech system. engine.say() puts a text into a queue, speaks nothing yet and returns None. engine.runAndWait() speaks everything in the queue and returns when the queue is empty. The book's first program, hello_tts.py, is these three calls. Slide 9 prints the events that arrive while the queue is spoken, and it also shows what a second call of runAndWait() does. See also the story on slide 7.

slides.title: Story: Kempelen published his speech research and a speaking machine in 1789
slides.say: Johann Wolfgang von Kempelen was a Hungarian writer, architect, engineer and inventor. He is known for The Turk, a chess playing hoax, and for a speaking machine that a hand played. In 1789 he published a book with nearly twenty years of his speech research, and an early version of the machine can be seen in the Deutsches Museum in Munich. The picture shows a reconstruction. pyttsx3 asks the speech system of the machine to do by program what that device did by hand, which slide 9 shows.

slides.title: Which versions run, and which tools are there?
slides.say: The first printed line is the version of Python, 3.14.6. The second is the list of versions: pyttsx3 2.99, openai-whisper 20250625, yt-dlp 2026.11.23 and numpy 2.5.4. All three packages change often, so a script should print what it ran with. ffmpeg and eSpeak NG are programs outside Python, and both were found on the PATH, which printed True twice. The device /dev/snd does not exist, so the machine has no sound card, which printed False. This is why the speech goes into files. Slide 9 continues with the engine.

slides.title: say() queues; runAndWait() speaks
slides.say: The engine's say() returned None and no event had arrived yet, so the queue only holds the text. After runAndWait() the list of events holds started and finished, one pair for the sentence. In the second box two child processes call runAndWait(). One call returned with exit 0. The process that called it twice was not back after 5 seconds, so a second runAndWait() in one process can wait for ever. Slide 6 explains the three calls, and the table on slide 39 lists this among the surprises.

slides.title: Part 2: Voices, rate, volume and WAV files
slides.say: Part 2 changes how the speech sounds and where it goes. The first example lists the voices of the speech system and chooses one by its id. The second example measures the effect of the rate and of the volume in the audio itself, by saying the same sentence at seven rates and at five volumes. The third example saves speech in a WAV file and reads its header, and it shows that the name of a file does not decide its format. Slide 11 explains the calls, and slide 12 tells the story of the Voder.

slides.title: Voices, properties and WAV files
slides.say: A property is a setting of the engine. getProperty() reads one of voices, voice, rate and volume, and setProperty() changes it for the speech that follows. A rate such as 300 is faster than the default of 200, and a volume is a number from 0.0 to 1.0. A voice is chosen from the list by its id. save_to_file() queues a text and a file name, and the WAV file is written when runAndWait() runs. A WAV file holds samples and a header with channels, sample size and rate. Related slides are 13, 14 and 15.

slides.title: Story: The Voder spoke at the 1939 New York World's Fair
slides.say: Homer Dudley invented the Voder at Bell Telephone Laboratories in 1937 and 1938, and it was shown at the 1939 New York World's Fair and in San Francisco. An operator used a wrist bar, keys and a foot pedal to make a buzz or a hiss into vowels, consonants and inflections. Helen Harper trained twenty operators. The picture shows the Voder with the crowd. The rate, the volume and the voice of slide 13 are settings of a program that the operator moved by hand.

slides.title: Voices: list, choose, save
slides.say: The engine listed 131 voices; the first is Afrikaans, with gender Male and age None, and its languages list is ['af']. The engine starts with the voice gmw/en. After setProperty('voice', voices[1].id) the sentence was saved as hello.wav, which is 1.48 seconds long. The voices belong to eSpeak NG, which is why a voice has a language code and a gender: a Windows or macOS machine lists other voices from SAPI5 or NSSpeechSynthesizer. Slide 11 explains getProperty() and setProperty(), and slide 14 saves the file.

slides.title: Rate and volume, measured in audio
slides.say: The sentence 'The quick brown fox jumps over the yellow lazy dog.' lasted 6.46 seconds at rate 50, 3.62 at 150, 1.76 at 300 and 1.26 at 400, so a higher rate makes shorter audio. The peak of the samples was 26394 at volume 1.0, 13024 at 0.5, 2222 at 0.1 and 0 at 0.0. Volume 5, which is outside the range, raised no error and gave 32768, the largest value of a 16-bit sample. Each measure used a fresh process. The strips draw rate 100 and rate 300 on one time scale. See slide 39.

slides.title: save_to_file() writes a WAV file
slides.say: Before runAndWait() the file did not exist, which printed False: save_to_file() only queues the request. The header of the written file says 1 channel, 2 bytes per sample and 22050 samples per second, and the sentence lasts 1.48 seconds. The second box saved a file named hello.mp3. It begins with the bytes RIFF and WAVE, so it is a WAV file with an mp3 name, and nothing was raised. The strip draws the samples of hello.wav. Slide 11 explains WAV, and the table on slide 39 lists this surprise.

slides.title: Part 3: Whisper: speech to text
slides.say: Part 3 turns audio into text. The first example loads three Whisper models and counts their parameters and the size of their files. The second example lets the machine's own speech be written back by each model and counts the wrong words. The third example shows that reading audio calls the ffmpeg program. The fourth example lets six sentences be heard in six languages and shows that the language is detected by the model. Slide 17 explains the calls, and slide 18 tells a story about speech recognition.

slides.title: Whisper: models and transcription
slides.say: Speech recognition makes text from spoken audio. whisper.load_model() loads a model by name, and the file of the model is downloaded on the first use. model.transcribe() returns a dictionary with the text, the language and a list of segments, and each segment has a start and an end time. Table 24-1 of the book lists the models tiny, base, small, medium and large with their sizes and speeds. Slide 19 measures the three smallest models on this machine, and slide 20 counts their wrong words.

slides.title: Story: Raj Reddy's group made computers understand connected speech
slides.say: Raj Reddy was born on 13 June 1937. He worked at Stanford and, from 1969, at Carnegie Mellon University on speech, language, vision and robotics. He and his colleagues made demonstrations such as voice control of a robot and large-vocabulary connected speech recognition. In 1994 he and Edward Feigenbaum received the ACM Turing Award. The picture shows him. The call model.transcribe() of slide 20 belongs to the same line of work, now with models that learned from large amounts of audio.

slides.title: Three models: parameters and file sizes
slides.say: Whisper has 14 model names. The three loaded here have 37.2 million parameters for tiny, 71.8 million for base and 240.6 million for small, and their files are 75572083, 145262807 and 483617219 bytes. The larger the model, the larger the file, which is the idea of Table 24-1 of the book. The machine has no graphics card, so cuda is False and the model runs on the cpu; asking for device='cuda' raised a RuntimeError. See slide 20 for what the size buys, and slide 17 for the calls.

slides.title: transcribe(): text, and how wrong it is
slides.say: The machine's own speech of the fox sentence was written back by three models with temperature 0.0 so that the run repeats. tiny wrote 'the quick run for some silver yellow laser dog.' with a word error rate of 0.6, and base and small wrote the sentence with a word error rate of 0.1. So the bigger models made fewer wrong words than tiny. The result is a dictionary with the keys text, segments and language, and each segment has keys such as id, seek, start and end. Compare slide 19 for the sizes and slide 28 for the writers.

slides.title: load_audio() calls the ffmpeg program
slides.say: load_audio() returned an array of 40970 numbers of type float32, which is the sentence at 16000 numbers for every second. With the PATH set to a folder that does not exist the same call raised FileNotFoundError, because load_audio() starts the program ffmpeg. The PATH was restored afterwards. The strip draws the audio as Whisper reads it. So a machine that runs Whisper needs ffmpeg as well as Python. Slide 8 printed that ffmpeg was found, and slide 21 follows with the languages.

slides.title: Whisper hears the language itself
slides.say: Three sentences were said by the eSpeak voice of each language and heard by two models. The tiny model detected the language of one sentence right out of three: it took Turkish for Thai and Italian for Korean. The base model was right for two of three; it also took Turkish for Thai. A language code that does not exist, xx, raised a ValueError. So the detected language is a guess of the model, and a small model guesses wrong more often. Compare slide 20, where size changed the words.

slides.title: Part 4: Subtitle files and downloaded audio
slides.say: Part 4 is about subtitles and downloads. The first example writes one result in three subtitle formats and compares each with the text of the book. The second example adds word times and lets the writer cut lines at a width. The third example reads the data of a web page without downloading the media. The fourth example downloads the audio and converts it, and it shows what happens with a wrong address. Slides 24 to 26 explain the calls, and slide 27 tells the story of closed captions.

slides.title: Subtitle files: SRT, VTT and TSV
slides.say: A subtitle file holds pieces of text, each with a start time and an end time. whisper.utils.get_writer() returns a function that writes a result in one format: srt, vtt, tsv, txt or json. The SRT format numbers its cues and writes the times with a comma before the milliseconds. The VTT format is the one of web pages, starts with the word WEBVTT and uses a point. The TSV format has the columns start, end and text, and its times are milliseconds. Slide 28 writes all three, and slide 29 adds word times.

slides.title: Downloading from a web page
slides.say: yt-dlp finds the media of a web page and downloads it. yt_dlp.YoutubeDL() makes the downloader from a dictionary of options. ydl.extract_info() reads the page and returns its data, and with download=False it fetches no media. ydl.sanitize_info() turns that data into plain types so that json.dumps() can write it as the file metadata.json. ydl.download() fetches the files of a list of addresses, and the book names the audio file downloaded_content.m4a. See slide 30 for the metadata and slide 31 for the download.

slides.title: Downloading from a page: the options
slides.say: The options of the downloader are a dictionary. 'skip_download': True reads the page and fetches no media. 'outtmpl' is a pattern for the file name, and %(ext)s becomes the real extension. 'format' lists what to prefer: m4a first, then the best audio, then the best of all. 'postprocessors' with FFmpegExtractAudio calls ffmpeg after the download to keep only the audio. 'quiet': True prints nothing while it works. Slide 31 uses these options, and compare slide 30 for the first one.

slides.title: Story: Closed captions were first shown in December 1971
slides.say: Closed captioning was first demonstrated in the United States in December 1971, at the First National Conference on Television for the Hearing Impaired in Knoxville, Tennessee. On 15 February 1972, at Gallaudet College, ABC and the National Bureau of Standards showed captions inside a normal broadcast of The Mod Squad. Regular open-captioned broadcasts began on PBS with The French Chef in 1972. The picture shows a caption. The SRT and VTT files of slide 28 carry the same kind of cue, with a start time and an end time.

slides.title: get_writer() writes SRT, VTT and TSV
slides.say: One result with two segments was written in three formats, and each file has the same text as the book's: srt 223 bytes, vtt 215 bytes and tsv 190 bytes. The SRT time is 00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:05,640 with a comma, the VTT time is 00:00.000 --> 00:05.640 with a point, and the TSV file has the columns start, end and text with milliseconds. A writer for docx does not exist, so get_writer('docx') raised a KeyError. The picture draws the two cues on a time axis. Slide 25 explains the formats.

slides.title: Word times make shorter cues
slides.say: The Gettysburg reading was transcribed by the tiny model. It gave 26 segments and the writer made 26 blocks. With word_timestamps=True the first segment has 14 words with their times, and with max_line_width=30 and max_line_count=2 the writer made 31 blocks. The first of them is printed. The tiny model wrote 'Liberal Vox' where the reader said LibriVox, so a small model also makes mistakes in names. The recording is hosted by the Internet Archive and stands in for a video. See slide 37.

slides.title: extract_info() reads the page, not the file
slides.say: The address is a page of the Internet Archive, not a video site, and yt-dlp reads it with the extractor archive.org. The title is The Gettysburg Address and there are 3 formats. Of the 13 keys that the book prints, 7 are present here; thumbnail, channel_id, channel_url, view_count, average_rating and age_limit are missing, because this page is not a video page. sanitize_info() made the dictionary safe, and metadata.json holds 55 keys. Slide 26 explains the calls, and slide 31 downloads the file.

slides.title: download() fetches the file and converts it
slides.say: The download returned 0, and the folder holds one file, downloaded_content.m4a, which ffprobe says is the codec aac and 100.3 seconds long. The options name the file with outtmpl, prefer m4a with format and convert with FFmpegExtractAudio. The second box shows two things: with one string instead of a list this yt-dlp also returned 0, and an address that is nowhere raised DownloadError. So a wrong address stops the program, and a script should catch it. Compare slide 38.

slides.title: Part 5: The practice programs
slides.say: Part 5 brings the parts together in three programs of the chapter. The first adds a voice to the game Guess the Number, so that every message is printed and saved as a WAV file. The second makes the verses of 99 Bottles of Beer and measures how long they are when spoken. The third is the transcriber: it downloads audio, transcribes it and writes the subtitle files for a list of addresses. Slide 33 explains the programs, and slides 34 and 37 tell two stories.

slides.title: The practice programs and the end of the chapter
slides.say: Three programs bring the chapter together. Adding Voice to Guess the Number speaks every message that the game prints. Singing 99 Bottles of Beer makes the verses of the song and speaks them. The YouTube Transcriber downloads the audio of a list of addresses, transcribes it and writes the subtitle files. The summary repeats the chapter in a few sentences, and the practice questions check it. Slides 35, 36 and 38 show the three programs run, and slides 40 and 41 are the questions and the summary.

slides.title: Story: A computer sang Daisy Bell in 1961
slides.say: Harry Dacre wrote the song Daisy Bell in 1892. It is the earliest song sung with computer speech synthesis, by an IBM 7090 in 1961. The picture shows that kind of machine. The program of slide 35 makes the 99 verses of another song and has a synthesizer speak them, and it writes the sound into a WAV file instead of playing it.

slides.title: A game whose every message is spoken
slides.say: The first box makes speak(), which prints a message and then queues it with save_to_file() and runs the queue, so that each message becomes a WAV file. The game was played with the guesses 5, 18 and 12 and a secret of 12, and it printed four messages, of which the second is '5 is too low.' The four files last 2.57, 1.09, 1.1 and 0.92 seconds. The pyttsx3 engine printed a line for each file it saved. Compare slide 9 for runAndWait().

slides.title: One text of 99 verses, spoken
slides.say: bottles() and verse() make the text of one verse; the last verse says 1 bottle and then No more bottles. Three verses lasted 18.69 seconds as a WAV file, and the 99 verses lasted 708.3 seconds, which is 11 minutes and 48 seconds. The strip draws the three verses. Compare slide 15, where a WAV file was read, and see the story on slide 34.

slides.title: Story: Lincoln spoke at Gettysburg on 19 November 1863
slides.say: Abraham Lincoln spoke on the afternoon of 19 November 1863 at the dedication of the Soldiers' National Cemetery at Gettysburg, four and a half months after the battle. Five manuscript copies are known, named after the people who received them, and the Bliss copy is the standard text. The picture shows a copy. The transcriber of slide 38 reads a public-domain recording of the address that the Internet Archive hosts, and that recording stands in for a video site.

slides.title: Many addresses to subtitles: one function
slides.say: transcribe_urls() does what the YouTube Transcriber does: for each address it downloads the audio, transcribes it with the language en and temperature 0.0, and writes a file in each format. The two readings of the Gettysburg Address gave 26 and 17 segments. One address that does not exist raised DownloadError, so a loop over many addresses should catch the error for each address. Both readings are hosted by the Internet Archive and stand in for a video site. See slides 30 and 31.

slides.title: Four surprises, measured by the run
slides.say: The table collects four results that the run measured. A second runAndWait() raised nothing and did not come back in 5 seconds. A file named hello.mp3 begins with RIFF and WAVE, so it is a WAV file. A volume of 5 raised nothing, and the peak was 32768 against 26394 at 1.0. download() with one string returned a value and not an error, although the book passes a list. None of the four raised an exception, so the script has to check the result itself. Compare slide 9 for the second runAndWait(), slide 15 for the file name, and slide 31 for the download.

slides.title: Practice Questions
slides.say: These are the practice questions, and each points to the part where the idea was shown. The first is about say(), runAndWait() and a second call, slides 8 and 9. The second is about the rate and a volume above 1.0, slide 14. The third is about the three models and what load_audio() needs, slides 20 and 21. The fourth is about SRT and VTT times and the value that download() returns, slides 28 and 31. The fifth is about the spoken messages of the game and the transcriber, slides 35 and 38.

slides.title: Summary
slides.say: Four claims carry the chapter. say() queues text and runAndWait() speaks it, and save_to_file() writes a WAV file when it runs. Rate, volume and voice are properties, and the run measured their effect in the audio. Bigger Whisper models make fewer wrong words, and reading audio needs ffmpeg. A writer makes SRT, VTT or TSV, yt-dlp reads and downloads from a web page, and several calls fail quietly. These answer the two questions of slide 3.

slides.title: Resources: where to go next
slides.say: These sixteen links are where to go next. They include the chapter of the book, the documentation and package pages of pyttsx3, Whisper and yt-dlp, the pages of FFmpeg and eSpeak NG, the Internet Archive reading that the examples use, and the pages behind the six stories. On 2026-11-27, thirteen of the sixteen pages were opened; the three GitHub pages could not be opened from the machine that built the deck, and the check log records this. Use the package pages for the newest versions, because all three packages change often. Compare the story slides 7, 12, 18, 27, 34 and 37, which carry the links to their pages.
